html:
Arkaim is a fortified settlement of the Sintashta culture in the steppe of the southern Urals, in Russia's Chelyabinsk region, built around 2000 BCE. Archaeologists found it in 1987, just before the valley was to be flooded for a reservoir, and the find saved it.

It was a round town about 160 metres across, with two rings of walls and houses built against them, all opening onto a central square. Like other sites of the Sintashta culture, it worked copper and bronze, and the culture's graves hold some of the earliest spoke wheeled chariots.

Most scholars link the Sintashta people to the early speakers of Indo-Iranian languages, whose descendants later moved south into Iran and India and composed the Rigveda. That link has drawn nationalist and New Age claims that Arkaim was the homeland of the Aryans or an ancient observatory, which archaeologists reject. Today it is an open air museum, and a pilgrimage site for some of those believers.
